speaker: fizzwick
text: Pip, Fizzwick has noticed you never sleep. Fizzwick finds this suspicious, and quietly admirable.

speaker: pip
text: Another fight. Finally, someone who says what they mean.

speaker: pip
text: Stay behind me. Not because I'm brave. Because I'm cheaper to replace.

speaker: pip
text: Right. Stab first, feelings never.

speaker: pip
text: One down. A few thousand grudges to go.

speaker: pip
text: Don't look so surprised. I've had practice.

speaker: pip
text: Right between the ribs. I'd say sorry, but I'd be lying.

speaker: pip
text: Lovely. I'd call it personal, but it never is.

speaker: pip
text: Ow. Noted. Adding it to the list.

speaker: pip
text: Oi! That was my good side. I have one.

speaker: pip
text: I'm fine. It's a flesh wound and a moral failing.

speaker: pip
text: Not dying today. I have an appointment.

speaker: pip
text: Get up. You don't get to die before I get my revenge. Wait, that's my line.

speaker: pip
text: Hey. Hey! Stay with us. I've buried enough friends.

speaker: pip
text: Money. The only friend who never sold me out.

speaker: pip
text: Shiny. Mine. Ours. Fine, ours, but I'm holding it.

speaker: pip
text: Down we go. Every step is closer to a conversation I've rehearsed for three years.

speaker: pip
text: Stairs. Of course. Nothing good ever lives upstairs.

speaker: pip
text: I'll take first watch. I don't sleep much anyway.

speaker: pip
text: Wake me if anything dies. Or if anything's about to.

speaker: pip
text: Oh, wonderful. Someone's been busy.

speaker: pip
text: Ow. Whoever built this, I'd love to shake their hand. Slowly. Around the neck.

speaker: pip
text: Told you. I'm a delight in a crisis.

speaker: pip
text: That's that. Anyone have a list of who's next?

speaker: pip
text: Sharper, faster, angrier. A balanced diet.

speaker: pip
text: A hidden door. I love hidden doors. They never pretend to be anything else.

speaker: pip
text: I'll check the corners. People hide things there. I used to.

speaker: pip
text: New room. Same old tower. Same old liars.

speaker: pip
text: Lantern Row Crew. Eleven of us. Best pockets in Emberhollow. We never robbed anybody who couldn't afford it. Mostly.

speaker: pip
text: Do you know the worst part of being betrayed? It isn't the betrayal. It's that I admired his handwriting.

speaker: pip
text: Brambur keeps apologising to the monsters. I keep not apologising to anyone. We balance out.

speaker: pip
text: Fizzwick talks about himself in the third person. I talk about everyone else in the past tense. We're both coping.

speaker: pip
text: My sister used to say revenge is a dish best served warm, because cold food gives you indigestion. She was seven. She was right.

speaker: grumsh
text: Pip does not speak of what was lost. I know that silence. I have written four hundred lines about the same one.

speaker: nettle
text: Easy. I once fought a hundred of these with a teapot.

speaker: nettle
text: I was married to a queen for a week. It ended over a disagreement about a throne. Hers. It was a very good throne.

speaker: pip
text: Nice room. Plenty of places to hide a knife.

speaker: pip
text: Quiet. I hate quiet. Quiet is when people are planning something.

speaker: pip
text: Good bones. Terrible company, I assume.

speaker: pip
text: Coin. Warm, reliable, never asks questions.

speaker: pip
text: Take it. Everything in a place like this was stolen from someone anyway.

speaker: pip
text: A hidden door. The only honest thing in this tower.

speaker: pip
text: Ha. Called it. Quietly. In my head. Every time.

speaker: pip
text: That one is big. Good. I am in a mood.

speaker: pip
text: I'll go around the back. It's where I do my best work.

speaker: pip
text: No. Not you too. I have done this before and I hated it.

speaker: pip
text: Not Brambur. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Fizzwick. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Grumsh. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Zizzy. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Vexrath. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Nettle. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Liora. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Not Ser Aldric. Not like this. Somebody get a healer. Somebody get me a healer, my hands are shaking.

speaker: pip
text: Emberhollow. Smells like bread, smoke and old lies. Home.

speaker: pip
text: Take a good look at it. Somebody in this town is still hiding something.

speaker: pip
text: Lantern Row Crew. Eleven of us, every one a thief. We never robbed anyone who couldn't spare it.

speaker: pip
text: Three years ago it was eleven. Now it is me. I'll tell you why when I'm ready, or drunk.

speaker: pip
text: My sister Posy was seven when she learned to pick a lock. She picked mine. I'd locked her out for being too loud.

speaker: pip
text: She's the reason I am still down here. Do not make it a thing.

speaker: pip
text: My partner was Garrick Vane. He taught me to open any lock with a hairpin and any person with a smile.

speaker: pip
text: Both lessons have since been used on me. Excellent teacher.

speaker: pip
text: The night the Row burned, I smelled lamp oil before I smelled smoke. Somebody poured it. Somebody had a key.

speaker: pip
text: I have replayed that night ten thousand times. It always ends with Garrick, smiling.

speaker: pip
text: When we find him, let me talk first. After that, you can have your turn, if there is anything left.

speaker: pip
text: If I get this wrong, tell Posy I was funny. I would like to be remembered as funny.

speaker: pip
text: Lovely party. Everyone smiling. I never trust a room where everyone is smiling.

speaker: pip
text: He took the Princess. Fine. I have been waiting years for a reason to go down there.

speaker: narrator
text: Back in Emberhollow, in the Boar & Spoon, which still smells faintly of smoke, Elowen draws Dawnfang and lays it on your shoulder.

speaker: pip
text: Malthrax is down. Garrick is still out there somewhere. Do not look so worried. I am patient.

speaker: narrator
text: Behind a heap of gnawed barrels, someone has chalked a lantern with four rays on the stone. The chalk is old. The dust around it is not.

speaker: pip
text: Don't touch that. That is the Lantern Row mark. My crew's. We left it wherever it was safe to leave things.

speaker: narrator
text: A halfling thieves' mark, the kind guild runners leave to say a place is safe. Someone down here knew the code.

speaker: narrator
text: A loose stone. Behind it, a folded cult payment slip. Forty sovereigns, paid to G. Vane, for the Row.

speaker: pip
text: G. Vane. Garrick Vane. He crosses his sevens like a man signing a death warrant. Three years I have wondered who sold us. Now I have a name, and a handwriting. Thank you for not making it a speech.

speaker: narrator
text: Somebody named G. Vane was paid forty sovereigns for something called the Row. Whatever that is, it sounds like a sale.

speaker: narrator
text: You find a stone that moves, and a slip of paper that dissolves at a touch. Three words survive: paid to G. Vane.

speaker: pip
text: Garrick. Of course it is Garrick. He always bought cheap paper. It is the one thing I would have trusted him on.

speaker: narrator
text: Half sunk in the shallows lies a child's rowboat, painted with the lantern mark. The name on the stern is nearly gone: P, O, S, Y.

speaker: pip
text: That is her boat. I painted it. Badly. She said it looked like a pudding. She named it herself, at seven years old, and she had opinions.

speaker: narrator
text: A child's boat, painted with a thief's mark and a girl's name. Somebody small once loved it.

speaker: narrator
text: Boot prints, deep, from a robed figure carrying something small. They lead to a landing, and a ledger page stuck in the mud: tithe received, one halfling girl, unharmed, for the Seneschal's own.

speaker: pip
text: Unharmed. Alive. She was alive. Excuse me. Something in my eye. The dungeon is very dusty.

speaker: narrator
text: A tithe slip. One halfling girl, unharmed, for the Seneschal's own. The cult took a living child.

speaker: narrator
text: The mud has swallowed whatever there was to find. You manage only a scrap of blue ribbon, caught on the oar.

speaker: pip
text: She wore one just like it. Either they took her, or she lost it. I would like to believe the first. It is the better story.

speaker: narrator
text: A wall of green crystal, scratched with a cult cipher. A column of names and numbers. One line is underlined twice.

speaker: pip
text: That is a tithe ledger. Names and prices. I know this hand. I would know it in the dark.

speaker: narrator
text: The cipher unravels. Seneschal of Keys, Garrick Vane, keeper of every door in the vault. And below it: Posy T. held in the servants' ward, to be returned when the Row is quiet.

speaker: pip
text: Seneschal. A title and a ring of keys, for eleven of us. And he kept her. Three years he has kept her, to make sure I stayed quiet.

speaker: narrator
text: The cipher fights you. You catch a title, Seneschal, and a name, Vane, before the rest swims away.

speaker: pip
text: Seneschal. Fancy. I would have given him a better title. Several.

speaker: narrator
text: At a cold forge, a Lantern Row key lies half finished in a clay mould, beside a note on cult stationery. Hurry the keys. The Sovereign's patience is thin, and so is mine. G.V.

speaker: pip
text: A master key, Lantern Row pattern. He is having them copied. He is making himself a way out. Coward.

speaker: narrator
text: Quick fingers, soft wax. When you lift your hand, the cast is perfect, and no one is the wiser. In the bow of the key, a pair of initials.

speaker: pip
text: G.V. In the bow. He signs his keys. Vain to the end.

speaker: narrator
text: The wax cracks, the mould shatters, and the key stays where it was. You pocket the note instead.

speaker: pip
text: Close enough. I know his handwriting. I know his keys. I will know his face when I see it.

speaker: narrator
text: Near the vault stair, a lantern hangs in an alcove, still burning. A Lantern Row lamp. Eleven notches are cut into the iron, one for each of the Crew.

speaker: pip
text: Eleven notches. One for each of us. He kept them. Garrick keeps everything. Sentimental. It is the worst thing about him.

speaker: narrator
text: Beyond the alcove stands a brass door worked with lanterns. The Seneschal's counting room, you think. It will open for anyone who is not afraid of what is behind it.

speaker: narrator
text: You light the lantern again, and carry the flame to the brass door.

speaker: narrator
text: A brass door worked with lantern marks, and a keyhole built for small hands. Some quarrels are not yours to settle alone. Pip belongs here, and Pip is not with you.

speaker: narrator
text: A brass door worked with lantern marks. A whole story is written on it, and you have missed the first pages. Look for Lantern Row marks on the floors above.

speaker: narrator
text: Gold light from a brazier. Ledgers stacked to the rafters. A man in a grey coat, with a ring of keys at his belt as long as your arm, writes without looking up.

speaker: garrick
text: Pip. You are late. I had you down for two winters ago. Do sit. Everyone sits eventually.

speaker: pip
text: Hello, Garrick. You have gone grey. It suits you. It is the first honest thing you have worn.

speaker: garrick
text: Come now. It was only business. The Row was never going to survive the Sovereign. I chose the winning side, and sold what was already lost.

speaker: pip
text: You sold eleven of us. And my sister.

speaker: narrator
text: Pip's hand is on a knife. Garrick's hands are open on the desk. Behind you, the door has swung shut on its own. Roll if you want answers, and know the whole table is watching.

speaker: narrator
text: You watch his hands, not his face. A tremor in his left thumb, the thing he always did when he would rather not say. He is not lying about the fire. He is lying by leaving something out.

speaker: garrick
text: She is not in the ash, Pip. I did that much. I did that much, and you may hate me for the rest.

speaker: narrator
text: He is very good. Every line lands calm, every pause is rehearsed. Whatever lies beneath it, you cannot find it.

speaker: garrick
text: She burned with the others. I am sorry. I think of her every day. I think of her often.

speaker: narrator
text: Pip's jaw tightens. He believes it, and perhaps you should too.

speaker: narrator
text: You set the cast down: a Lantern Row key, newly forged, with Garrick's own initials in the bow. He looks at it the way a man looks at his own gravestone.

speaker: garrick
text: Well. You have been thorough. Very well. She is not dead. I hid her before the fire. I was never a good man, Pip. I was a careful one.

speaker: narrator
text: There are no more questions. The guards are gone, the keys lie on the desk, and a knife is in Pip's hand. Everyone at the table is looking at you.

speaker: pip
text: It is your call. It was always going to be your call. I just want you to know I have already made up my mind.

speaker: narrator
text: Vengeance or mercy. There is no die for this one.

speaker: narrator
text: You nod, and say nothing. Pip does not say a word either. It is quick, and cleaner than Garrick deserved.

speaker: garrick
text: Pip. She is...

speaker: narrator
text: He does not finish the sentence. The keys hit the floor, and the whole ring rings like a bell.

speaker: pip
text: That is it? Three years. That is all there was?

speaker: narrator
text: Garrick said Posy was alive, and the only man who knew where is on the floor. The strongbox holds three hundred gold, a ledger of every name the Row ever sold, and a plain dagger forged from a Lantern Row lamp.

speaker: pip
text: He took her with him. Of course he did. I will find her. It will just take longer.

speaker: narrator
text: The strongbox holds three hundred gold, a ledger of every name the Row ever sold, and a plain dagger forged from a Lantern Row lamp.

speaker: pip
text: Keep the gold. I will take the dagger, and the ledger. Someone should remember their names.

speaker: narrator
text: You say stop. Pip hears you, and does not stop. It is quick, and nobody in the room says a word afterwards.

speaker: pip
text: I heard you. I am sorry. I could not do it your way.

speaker: narrator
text: Put it down, you say, and for a long moment, nothing. Then the knife trembles, and drops point first into the desk, quivering.

speaker: pip
text: Fine. Fine! I hate this. I am letting him live because you asked, not because he deserves it.

speaker: garrick
text: Posy is alive. She is in Emberhollow, a lamplighter's apprentice on Cant Street, under the name Pell. And here is something you do not know. The Sovereign's staff has a crack beneath the third ring. Strike there, and the whole thing shatters.

speaker: narrator
text: Garrick goes in chains. Pip does not look at him once. The whole way back up the stair, Pip does not say a word.

speaker: narrator
text: Fenn and Daughters, Pawnbrokers, sits crooked between the smithy and the temple. The shutters are closed at noon, which is unheard of. A bell jangles as you enter.

speaker: odalys
text: Shut the door. Quickly. Someone is selling cult silver in Emberhollow, temple candlesticks with the Blackspire sigil filed off, and every pawn ticket bears my name. I never wrote them.

speaker: odalys
text: Captain Rowan will see a cult fence, not a victim, if he sees those tickets before I clear this. Find who is forging my hand, and I will make it worth your while.

speaker: odalys
text: Because Rowan would hang the nearest thief and call it justice. I have pawned since I was fourteen. I know how magistrates think.

speaker: narrator
text: Odalys slides three things across the counter: a forged ticket, a smear of grave dirt on a handkerchief, and a candle stub that smells of lilies. Where you start is up to you.

speaker: narrator
text: Three threads, one forger. Pull them in any order. Roll well, and the town starts to talk.

speaker: narrator
text: The ink is Odalys's, but the loops are wrong. The forger is left handed and smudged every final letter. The paper smells faintly of lilies and damp earth.

speaker: narrator
text: You squint until the loops swim. A forgery, certainly, but the ink gives nothing else away. Odalys wrings her hands.

speaker: narrator
text: The night watchman eyes your coin, then your face, then talks. A stooped figure with a spade and a lantern has crossed Cant Street after the third bell, three nights running, always toward the pawnshop.

speaker: narrator
text: The watchman clams up. Questions about grave dirt make him nervous, and he suggests you take them elsewhere. A round of drinks might have helped. It costs you ten gold anyway.

speaker: narrator
text: Crouched behind a rain barrel, you wait. After the bell, a stooped man with a spade slips a candlestick through the pawnshop's coal hatch, whistling a hymn off key. Dirt crumbles from his boots. He never sees you.

speaker: narrator
text: Your knee cracks like a dry twig. A shape in the alley freezes, then bolts, leaving behind the smell of lilies and nothing more.

speaker: narrator
text: Odalys has found her nerve, and a lantern. Everyone in the shop is waiting for a name. Three people could have done this. Choose carefully, and know that a wrong name costs her dearly.

speaker: narrator
text: Your suspect proves their innocence quickly, loudly, and in front of witnesses. Odalys apologises to everyone and pays for the trouble. It stings her purse, and her pride.

speaker: narrator
text: You find Tuck Harrow in the churchyard at dusk, leaning on his spade, a lantern at his feet. Dirt on his boots. Lilies on his hat.

speaker: tuck
text: Bit late for a stroll, friends. Looking for someone to bury?

speaker: narrator
text: You lay the evidence out on a headstone. His smile fades. He sits down hard on a grave.

speaker: tuck
text: It was the candlesticks. The old spares, sat in the crypt since before the Sovereign. Nobody counts the dead's candlesticks. I owe three months rent, and my wife is poorly. I used Mistress Fenn's name because it was the only name a pawnbroker would trust. I am sorry. I am so sorry.

speaker: narrator
text: Odalys, at your elbow, has gone very pale. The choice, and the consequence, are yours.

speaker: narrator
text: Captain Rowan's men come at dawn. Tuck goes quietly, and the town sleeps easier, though a gravedigger's wife weeps on Cant Street all that week.

speaker: odalys
text: Justice is done. It feels like less than I had hoped. Take the cloak. It was never redeemed.

speaker: tuck
text: I will dig your garden and sweep your shop, Mistress, for a year and a day. And I will pay back every coin.

speaker: odalys
text: A year and a day. And you tell no one where you found those candlesticks. I would like the Temple to go on believing that crypt is sealed.

speaker: narrator
text: The town never learns. Odalys sleeps well, and Tuck's wife is soon sitting up in bed, thanks to a physician Odalys quietly pays.

speaker: narrator
text: Tuck bolts over the churchyard wall and is gone before you can blink. Odalys sits among the graves and laughs, a short, tired laugh.

speaker: odalys
text: Well. The thieving stops, at least. I will cover the tickets myself. Take something for your trouble.

speaker: narrator
text: You name a price for your silence, and Tuck pays it in coin he cannot spare.

speaker: odalys
text: I did not see that, and I did not hear that, and we will never speak of it. Here. Your half of the quiet.

speaker: tuck
text: No. I have buried better folk than you. Go on, tell the Captain. See if he believes a pawnbroker's ledger over a gravedigger's word.

speaker: narrator
text: Odalys is trembling. Tuck is waiting, and so is the night.

speaker: odalys
text: Well? The tickets will not forge themselves, though someone seems determined to try.

speaker: odalys
text: Fenn and Daughters remembers a kindness. Come back any time. There is always a bargain behind the counter.

speaker: narrator
text: Harl Tollow mends nets on the Emberhollow wharf, though no boat has gone out in a month. He does not look up until your shadow falls across the cord.

speaker: harl
text: You are the ones going down. Aye. My wife Anselma led the Sisters of the Tide, fourteen voices, every dusk at the old shrine in the grotto. The cult came for the shrine. The Sisters went down to sing, and never came up.

speaker: harl
text: Some nights I hear them through the cellar wall, singing the Evening Hymn, only slower. Find out what happened. Bring me my wife, or bring me the truth. I will take either.

speaker: narrator
text: Harl presses his wife's silver brooch into your palm. It is cold as pond water. So you know them, he says, and so they know you.

speaker: harl
text: The tide is still turning. Any word of Anselma?

speaker: harl
text: She is free? Truly free? Then I will sleep tonight. It is not much, but it is hers: Anselma's mantle, and every coin I could scrape. She would say you should have a hot meal.

speaker: narrator
text: He weeps without embarrassment, and hums a few bars of the Evening Hymn, badly.

speaker: narrator
text: Harl hears you out with his hands folded around the net cord. He does not weep. That is worse.

speaker: harl
text: She is still singing. Still down there. You made a bell of my wife.

speaker: harl
text: Take your silver and go. I will not say it was wrong. I will not say thank you either.

speaker: harl
text: The nets are full again, and some evenings I sing the hymn myself. Badly. She would laugh.

speaker: harl
text: I hear her through the cellar wall, still. I do not go down there.

speaker: narrator
text: A stair of slick stone leads to a half drowned chapel. Fourteen benches stand in the black water. A hymnal lies open on a lectern, its pages swollen but still legible. Somewhere beneath the floor, a woman is humming.

speaker: narrator
text: A clever party rolls before it touches anything.

speaker: narrator
text: The last verse is in a different hand, written in haste. Sing me out, if you love me. The deep wants a choir, and we are all the choir it will get. It is a binding rite. Sung backwards, it would also release.

speaker: narrator
text: The ink has run into a blue bruise. You catch a word here and there: sing, deep, hold. Enough to be afraid, not enough to be useful.

speaker: narrator
text: The humming does not come from the water. It comes from the lectern's brass bell, and when you lean close, a voice speaks from it.

speaker: anselma
text: Do not let Harl come down. Please. He will wade in after me, and the Pool will keep him too. Tell him I am not afraid. Tell him I lied.

speaker: narrator
text: The humming slides away from you like a fish. You hear only the water lapping at fourteen empty benches.

speaker: narrator
text: You close the hymnal gently. Beyond the chapel, a passage slopes down toward cold, black water.

speaker: narrator
text: A black pool, perfectly still, ringed by fourteen stone posts. Something sings beneath it. You decide you are not ready. The chapel might have answers.

speaker: narrator
text: Fourteen shapes hang in the water below you, robed and swaying. Their mouths open and close in the Evening Hymn. In the middle, tied to a rotted post, a bell as wide as a cartwheel rings without a clapper. A woman's face drifts nearest the surface.

speaker: anselma
text: Harl. Is that Harl? No. Thank the Tide. Listen. The Sisters are bound to the bell. The cult did it to hold the grotto water back from the vault, and we have sung until we forgot we may stop. I cannot stop on my own.

speaker: narrator
text: You may free them, or you may take the Choir for yourselves. Either way, the bell needs a hand on it, and the water does not like that.

speaker: narrator
text: The water surges and drags at your ankles. Cold bites to the bone. Everyone takes six damage before the Pool lets go.

speaker: narrator
text: You sing the last verse backwards, one note at a time. The bell rings once, a clean, ordinary sound, and stops. Fourteen lights rise from the water like lanterns, and one of them lingers at your shoulder.

speaker: anselma
text: Thank you. Tell Harl the brooch is his. Tell him to go fishing.

speaker: narrator
text: The Pool is only water now. The way is clear.

speaker: narrator
text: You take up the Choir's thread and pull it taut. Fourteen faces turn toward you, empty and obedient. The bell speaks in a voice like cold iron, and it is yours.

speaker: anselma
text: No. Please. Not like this.

speaker: narrator
text: She does not stop singing. The Sisters will fight for you, now, wherever there is water to fight in. Whether they would have wished it is another question. The bell's iron heart drops into your hands.

speaker: narrator
text: In a seam of green crystal, a woman in a scorched leather apron sits with her knees drawn up and a hammer in her fist. She flinches at your torch, then lowers the hammer an inch.

speaker: ysolde
text: Do not shine that at me. They bring lights, and then they bring questions. Are you the heroes the cult keeps whispering about? The ones who killed Skarn?

speaker: ysolde
text: Ysolde Verrin. Third generation, Glimmerdeep Glassworks. The cult took us all for the Sovereign's commission: a mirror, tall as a door, to watch whoever came down the stair. I ground the lens. I am so sorry. It is in the old kiln, east of here, and it is looking at you right now.

speaker: narrator
text: Her eyes flick to the crystal over your shoulder. In it, faint and wrong, your party's reflection looks back, one beat late.

speaker: ysolde
text: Break it, or learn from it. I will not tell you which. A glasswright learns what a mirror costs, and I have paid. Go to the kiln. I will wait here. I am very good at waiting.

speaker: narrator
text: She will not believe you, not until you leave a flask of water and twenty gold at her feet. That seems to do it.

speaker: ysolde
text: Fine. Ysolde Verrin, glasswright. I made the cult a scrying mirror, under duress, and it stands in the old kiln east of here. It watches. Break it or use it. I just want it gone from my sight.

speaker: ysolde
text: Well? The kiln is east. Do not look into it too long. It is rude, and it looks back.

speaker: narrator
text: The kiln is a brick cavern, warm for the first time in a week. In the middle stands the Mirror, tall as a door, framed in black iron. The glass shows the room as it will be in an hour: your party, exactly where you stand, and your faces, tired.

speaker: narrator
text: It wants something from you. Mirrors always do.

speaker: narrator
text: You trace the iron frame with a steady finger. Ten runes, each ending in an eye. It sees what we see, you realise, and reports it to the vault below. Break it and the Sovereign loses an eye. Gaze long enough, and you will see through it. You will also be seen.

speaker: narrator
text: Your reflection grabs your wrist, cold as a river stone, and lets go. Everyone takes four damage from the cold.

speaker: narrator
text: The hammer rebounds as if from a drum. Shock shivers up your arm. Everyone takes five damage as the Mirror laughs, soundlessly.

speaker: narrator
text: The hammer comes down. The Mirror does not break so much as sigh. Ten eyes go dark, one by one, and a thousand silver shards rain across the kiln floor. Far beneath the vault, something large snarls, and cannot say why.

speaker: narrator
text: You look. The glass ripples, then clears. A long table lit by violet fire. A crown of black iron. A staff with a crack beneath the third ring. And then the Sovereign turns his head, and looks straight back at you.

speaker: malthrax
text: Little heroes. I have been waiting.

speaker: narrator
text: The glass goes dark. You know where to strike the staff. He knows your faces. Somewhere above, a seal cracks, and you glimpse the cache of the Glassworks guild, three hundred gold left behind.

speaker: ysolde
text: It is quiet. The glass hums no more. Take this. Verrin glass, ground for you. It will keep the world's tricks out of your eyes.

speaker: narrator
text: She laughs, a little wildly, and sets down her hammer for the first time in months.

speaker: ysolde
text: You looked. Of course you looked. Everyone looks. I will not lecture. I will only say the Mirror still stands, and it knows your faces now. Be quick.

speaker: narrator
text: In the cold ash of a collapsed barracks, a pale man in a Warden's tabard stands at attention before a wall of scratched names. He does not blink. Frost forms on your armour as you approach.

speaker: crane
text: Halt. Name and watch. No. You are not Watch. You are too loud and too alive.

speaker: crane
text: Sergeant Aldous Crane, Warden's Watch, Fourth Company. I call the roll every night, and every night three names do not answer. Corporal Dunstan Hale. Private Ilsa Marn. Private Joss Kettering. I cannot rest until I know where they lie, and why the seals fell on my watch.

speaker: narrator
text: He says why the seals fell on my watch too quickly, the way a man says a thing he has said to himself a thousand times. Whatever happened, the Sergeant suspects someone he loved.

speaker: narrator
text: His face gives you nothing, not even breath. A man long dead keeps his secrets well.

speaker: crane
text: Then you have my thanks, and my sword arm, if the dead can lend one. They will be deeper. The Fourth's barracks were on the vault level. Look for our tags.

speaker: narrator
text: Deep in the vault, the Watch's barracks has survived untouched: a ring of bunks and a wall of names. Three tags hang on three rusted nails. Each has a story, and each is worth a roll.

speaker: narrator
text: Her bunk is neat. A letter lies under the pillow. Dunstan told me to guard the north seal. He said the Sergeant ordered it. The Sergeant never did.

speaker: narrator
text: A neat bunk, a folded blanket, dust. Whatever Ilsa Marn left behind, she left it somewhere else.

speaker: narrator
text: Joss Kettering died of a blade in the back, not the front. The sheath on his belt carries Dunstan's initials.

speaker: narrator
text: The tags are brittle and the bones beneath are long past telling stories. Whatever killed him, you cannot say.

speaker: narrator
text: The lock gives. Inside, a ledger of seal rotas in Dunstan's hand, and a purse of Sovereign's gold, minted before Malthrax ever rose.

speaker: narrator
text: The lock jams, and a needle springs from the hasp. Everyone takes four damage as the poison burns off.

speaker: narrator
text: You gather what you have found. Behind you, the frost on the wall begins to creep.

speaker: narrator
text: Frost pools around a rusted gate. Someone is waiting beyond it, but you are not ready. The Fourth Company's barracks should have answers.

speaker: narrator
text: Sergeant Crane's ghost waits on a landing of black stone, his tabard bright with frost. The names on the wall behind you seem to be listening.

speaker: crane
text: You have found them. I see it in how you stand. Tell me, then. Where did Dunstan Hale fall, and who opened my seals?

speaker: narrator
text: The evidence in your hands is plain: Dunstan Hale opened the north seal for Sovereign's gold, and Joss Kettering died trying to stop him.

speaker: narrator
text: You have only fragments. Not proof. The Sergeant will know the difference.

speaker: crane
text: Fragments. I will not hang a dead man on fragments. Come back with more, or with a kinder story.

speaker: crane
text: Do not lie to a sergeant. I have heard a thousand excuses from better liars than you.

speaker: narrator
text: The cold bites. Everyone takes five damage.

speaker: narrator
text: You tell it plainly. Dunstan's gold. Joss's back. Ilsa's letter. The ghost listens without moving, until the frost on his tabard cracks like glass.

speaker: crane
text: Dunstan. My oldest friend. I would have given him my own pay. Thank you. I would rather know. A man should know who he held the line beside.

speaker: narrator
text: He draws a sword of pale light and turns toward the depths. His tabard glows, the Watch's colours, bright as dawn.

speaker: crane
text: I will stand with you at the end, if you will have me. Hold the line.

speaker: narrator
text: He held the line, you say. To the last. The Sergeant closes his eyes.

speaker: crane
text: To the last. Yes. That sounds like Dunstan. I will tell the others he held the line.

speaker: narrator
text: The frost melts. Crane salutes you, and the salute is the last thing you see before he is simply gone. On the step, he has left a pouch of old coin, and two vials. A debt, paid forward.

speaker: narrator
text: A note: "Lantern Row was here. Do not follow. Not sorry."

speaker: narrator
text: Dozens of tiny shrines line this room: thimbles, buttons and bent nails arranged with real devotion around a portrait of a very fat rat.
